title: Hyperthyroidism: Confirm Thyrotoxicosis, Then Identify the Cause
bottomLine: Hyperthyroidism management starts by confirming biochemical thyrotoxicosis and determining whether excess hormone is being synthesized or released from an inflamed gland. Graves disease, autonomous nodules and thyroiditis do not share the same definitive treatment, and thyroid storm is a clinical emergency rather than a laboratory threshold.
recognize: Heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, palpitations, frequent stool, anxiety and proximal weakness are common; older adults may present mainly with atrial fibrillation, weight loss or heart failure.
Graves disease may include diffuse goitre and orbitopathy, while nodular autonomy and thyroiditis have different patterns.
differentiate: Suppressed TSH with elevated free thyroid hormone confirms thyrotoxicosis, but etiology requires antibodies, scintigraphy or other cause-directed testing when not clinically obvious.
Thyroiditis releases preformed hormone and does not respond to antithyroid drugs like Graves/toxic nodular hyperthyroidism.
assessment: Assess HR/rhythm, heart failure, fever/CNS change, eye symptoms, goitre/nodules, pregnancy, iodine/amiodarone exposure and infection/other storm precipitants.
workup: Use TSH and free thyroid hormone testing; use receptor antibodies and thyroid scintigraphy when they answer the etiologic question and are appropriate to pregnancy/lactation status.
Do not substitute routine thyroid ultrasound for functional etiologic testing when the problem is thyrotoxicosis without a palpable structural indication.
management: Treat symptom burden and the specific cause using current thyroid-specialty guidance; Graves/toxic nodular disease may use antithyroid medication, radioiodine or surgery depending on patient factors.
Thyroid storm requires emergency multidrug acute-care management and treatment of the precipitant.
medicationSafety: Methimazole and propylthiouracil can cause agranulocytosis and liver injury; fever or significant sore throat requires urgent assessment rather than waiting for routine follow-up.
Pregnancy changes antithyroid-drug and definitive-treatment choices.
redFlags: Agranulocytosis or severe hepatic injury symptoms
counselling: Teach toxicity warning symptoms and explain that treatment depends on the cause of thyrotoxicosis, not only the hormone level.
followUp: Trend thyroid function at treatment-appropriate intervals and ensure a definitive long-term plan for Graves/autonomous disease.
examTrap: Escalating antithyroid medication in thyroiditis because free T4 remains high without establishing whether the gland is actually synthesizing excess hormone.
oneLinePearl: Thyrotoxicosis is the biochemical state; the cause determines the treatment.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada / Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism Endocrinology Recommendations

title: Thyroid Cancer Surveillance: Follow Risk and Response, Not One Universal Calendar
bottomLine: Thyroid-cancer follow-up is adapted to histology, initial stage/risk, treatment received and response over time. Surveillance may use neck examination, ultrasound and tumor markers such as thyroglobulin/antibodies for differentiated disease or calcitonin/CEA for medullary disease; do not apply the same test schedule to every survivor indefinitely.
recognize: New neck mass, persistent hoarseness, dysphagia, cough, bone pain or other new focal symptoms can signal recurrence and should not wait for the next routine visit.
Differentiated, medullary and anaplastic thyroid cancers have different markers, treatments and surveillance needs.
differentiate: Thyroglobulin interpretation depends on thyroid tissue/therapy, antibodies and assay context; it is not a general thyroid-cancer marker for every histology.
A stable low-risk survivor differs from a patient with biochemical or structural incomplete response and should not receive the same imaging intensity.
assessment: Review histology, surgery/RAI/systemic treatment, prior risk classification, current response category, TSH strategy, new symptoms, pregnancy plans and treatment sequelae.
workup: Use risk/response-adapted neck ultrasound and the appropriate tumor markers; reserve cross-sectional/nuclear imaging for clinically indicated higher-risk or discordant findings.
Confirm who owns surveillance and pending results after transition from oncology/endocrine specialty care.
management: Maintain thyroid-hormone therapy/TSH goals according to cancer risk and specialist plan while avoiding unnecessary long-term overtreatment in lower-risk disease.
Refer biochemical or structural recurrence, progressive symptoms or uncertain surveillance findings back to thyroid-cancer expertise.
medicationSafety: Excessive chronic TSH suppression can increase atrial-fibrillation and bone risks; the degree of suppression should match cancer risk and response rather than be universal.
Pregnancy changes thyroid-hormone requirements and surveillance logistics and needs coordinated follow-up.
counselling: Explain that thyroid cancer can require long-term surveillance but the intensity should change as recurrence risk and response become clearer.
followUp: Use the specialist-defined risk/response plan and close the loop on every ordered tumor marker or imaging result.
examTrap: Ordering the same annual scan panel forever for every thyroid-cancer survivor regardless of histology, risk and response.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid-cancer surveillance follows histology, recurrence risk and response—not a one-size-fits-all calendar.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cancer Society thyroid cancer follow-up resources

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism: Confirm PTH-Dependent Hypercalcemia Before Localizing
bottomLine: Primary hyperparathyroidism is a biochemical diagnosis of inappropriate PTH activity in the setting of confirmed hypercalcemia. Confirm calcium status and exclude important mimics/secondary causes before localization imaging; imaging localizes abnormal glands for surgery, it does not establish the diagnosis.
recognize: Many patients are asymptomatic, while others have nephrolithiasis, osteoporosis/fracture, constipation, polyuria, neurocognitive symptoms or kidney dysfunction.
Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia can cause dehydration, vomiting, confusion, arrhythmia and acute kidney injury.
differentiate: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia and medications such as lithium can mimic primary hyperparathyroidism.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism from CKD/vitamin D deficiency generally occurs without the same pattern of PTH-dependent hypercalcemia.
assessment: Review kidney stones, fractures, bone density, calcium/vitamin D intake, kidney disease, lithium/thiazides, family history and symptoms of severe hypercalcemia.
workup: Confirm total calcium corrected for albumin or ionized calcium as clinically appropriate, measure PTH and assess creatinine/eGFR, phosphate and 25-hydroxyvitamin D when indicated.
Use urinary calcium/family evaluation when FHH is plausible and obtain localization imaging only after the biochemical diagnosis when surgery is planned.
management: Refer surgical candidates for parathyroidectomy assessment using current endocrine/surgical criteria; monitor patients managed nonoperatively for calcium, renal and skeletal complications.
Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia requires urgent volume/calcium-lowering management and cause-directed care.
medicationSafety: Thiazides and lithium can affect calcium/PTH interpretation; review them before assigning etiology.
Do not treat vitamin D deficiency recklessly in marked hypercalcemia; repletion should be monitored and individualized.
counselling: Explain that imaging is for surgical planning after the biochemical diagnosis, not a screening test for hyperparathyroidism.
followUp: Track calcium, kidney function, stones and skeletal health; ensure surgical/pathology results close the loop when operated.
examTrap: Ordering a sestamibi scan to diagnose hyperparathyroidism before proving PTH-dependent hypercalcemia.
oneLinePearl: Biochemistry diagnoses primary hyperparathyroidism; imaging only tells the surgeon where to look.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada endocrine laboratory stewardship

title: Hypoparathyroidism: Control Symptoms Without Driving Hypercalciuria
bottomLine: Hypoparathyroidism causes inadequate PTH-mediated calcium regulation. Chronic management aims for symptom control and safe calcium/phosphate balance while avoiding hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis and overtreatment; acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is an emergency calcium/ECG pathway.
recognize: Perioral tingling, paresthesias, cramps, tetany, seizures and QT prolongation can occur with significant hypocalcemia.
Post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery is a common cause; autoimmune/genetic and magnesium-related causes also exist.
differentiate: Low magnesium can impair PTH secretion/action and make hypocalcemia refractory until magnesium is corrected.
Vitamin D deficiency and CKD can cause hypocalcemia with secondary PTH elevation rather than true hypoparathyroidism.
assessment: Review surgery history, symptoms, calcium/vitamin D therapy, kidney stones, kidney function, pregnancy, magnesium and medications that alter calcium.
workup: Use calcium/albumin or ionized calcium, phosphate, magnesium, creatinine/eGFR, PTH and vitamin D context to establish and monitor the disorder.
Monitor urine calcium/kidney imaging when chronic therapy or stone risk warrants it.
management: Use individualized calcium plus active vitamin D therapy under endocrine guidance, targeting symptom control without unnecessary high serum calcium.
Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia, seizure, laryngospasm or major ECG changes requires urgent IV calcium and monitored management.
medicationSafety: Excess calcium/calcitriol can cause hypercalciuria, stones and renal injury even when serum calcium is not dramatically high.
Correct significant magnesium deficiency when present because calcium may remain difficult to stabilize otherwise.
counselling: Teach consistent medication use, symptoms of low/high calcium and why chronic monitoring includes the kidneys, not just serum calcium.
followUp: Trend serum calcium/phosphate/magnesium and kidney/urine calcium risk according to stability, pregnancy and treatment changes.
examTrap: Escalating calcium repeatedly without checking magnesium or the renal consequences of chronic calcium/calcitriol therapy.
oneLinePearl: Treat hypoparathyroidism to safe physiology, not to a high-normal calcium target.

title: Vitamin D Deficiency: Test Selected Risk, Treat the Clinical Context
bottomLine: 25-hydroxyvitamin D testing is useful when deficiency risk or a bone/mineral disorder will change management; it is not a universal wellness screen. Treatment should match deficiency severity, calcium/bone context, absorption, kidney disease and pregnancy while avoiding unnecessary high-dose exposure.
recognize: Risk increases with limited sun exposure, malabsorption/bariatric disease, osteoporosis/fragility fracture, selected medications and other clinical contexts.
Severe deficiency can contribute to osteomalacia, muscle weakness and secondary hyperparathyroidism, but fatigue alone is nonspecific.
differentiate: Low vitamin D is not synonymous with osteoporosis and does not explain every pain/fatigue syndrome.
CKD and other mineral-bone disorders may require specialist interpretation of vitamin D/PTH/calcium/phosphate together.
assessment: Assess diet/supplement use, malabsorption, kidney/liver disease, fractures/falls, medications, pregnancy and calcium intake.
workup: Measure 25-hydroxyvitamin D when risk factors or a bone/mineral disorder make the result actionable; pair with calcium/phosphate/PTH and other tests when the differential requires it.
Avoid repeated testing in stable low-risk patients when it will not change therapy.
management: Use evidence-based supplementation/repletion appropriate to deficiency and clinical context, then transition to maintenance intake when corrected.
For routine bone health in adults over 50, align calcium/vitamin D nutrition with Health Canada/Osteoporosis Canada recommendations rather than megadose therapy.
medicationSafety: Excess vitamin D/calcium can cause hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria and kidney stones; avoid prolonged high-dose therapy without an indication and monitoring plan.
counselling: Explain that vitamin D is one part of skeletal health and more supplementation is not automatically better.
followUp: Repeat testing only when confirming correction or managing a high-risk disorder where the result changes treatment.
examTrap: Ordering vitamin D levels repeatedly for nonspecific fatigue in a low-risk patient and treating to an arbitrary very high target.
oneLinePearl: Test vitamin D when the answer changes care; treat deficiency without turning supplementation into toxicity.
sourceBasis: Health Canada vitamin D nutrition recommendations

title: Osteoporosis: Fracture Risk Drives Treatment More Than T-Score Alone
bottomLine: Canadian osteoporosis care is fracture-risk based. Identify fragility fractures and clinical risk factors, use BMD/FRAX appropriately, assess secondary causes, and choose pharmacotherapy according to fracture risk and patient factors rather than treating every low T-score identically.
recognize: Prior hip/vertebral or multiple fragility fractures markedly increase future fracture risk, especially soon after a fracture.
Falls, glucocorticoids, low body weight, smoking, parental hip fracture and secondary osteoporosis modify risk.
differentiate: Osteoporosis is not simply 'low calcium' and a normal serum calcium does not exclude high fracture risk.
Osteomalacia and other metabolic bone diseases require different evaluation/treatment.
assessment: Assess fracture/falls history, height loss, glucocorticoids, smoking/alcohol, secondary causes, kidney function, dental issues, calcium/vitamin D intake and patient preferences.
workup: Use Canadian FRAX with BMD when indicated and targeted biochemical testing for secondary causes/medication limitations.
Obtain vertebral imaging when clinical or risk criteria suggest occult vertebral fracture.
management: Bisphosphonates are first-line for most people initiating pharmacotherapy under the 2023 Osteoporosis Canada guideline; denosumab is an alternative when bisphosphonates are unsuitable, and selected very-high-risk patients merit osteoporosis-expert review for anabolic therapy.
Combine pharmacotherapy with balance/resistance exercise, falls prevention and adequate nutrition.
medicationSafety: Denosumab should not be delayed/stopped without a planned antiresorptive transition because rapid bone loss and vertebral fractures can occur.
Bisphosphonate suitability depends on renal/GI/dental and administration considerations; drug-holiday decisions apply to bisphosphonates, not denosumab in the same way.
counselling: Frame treatment around fracture prevention and function, not a single BMD score; explain the long-term plan before starting denosumab.
followUp: Reassess adherence, new fractures/risk factors and BMD at evidence-based intervals; investigate apparent treatment failure before simply escalating.
examTrap: Stopping denosumab without transition therapy or treating every T-score below -2.5 with the same medication regardless of fracture risk and contraindications.
oneLinePearl: Treat fracture risk, then choose the bone medication whose long-term plan you can safely complete.
sourceBasis: Osteoporosis Canada Clinical Practice Guideline for Management of Osteoporosis and Fracture Prevention — 2023 Update
